title: Yearly reports to the State that the organization's own tax return contradicts
question: Where a City-funded charity answered a Yes/No question on its yearly report to the Attorney General, does its own federal return for the same year say the same thing?
finding: 162 yearly reports from 66 organizations were read; 94 could be set beside the organization's e-filed tax return for the same year. 9 reports from 6 organizations answer "No" to transactions with officers or directors although the return for that year lists such transactions on Schedule L ($1.2 million in all), the largest at Project Wreckless for the year ended 2025-12-31 ($584,180). 14 answer "No" to government funding against the return or the City's ledger for the same twelve months, 6 claim an audit the return says was not done, and 4 answer "No" on restricted funds against the return's balance sheet.
how: Form RRF-1 is the yearly report a charity signs under penalty of perjury and sends to the Attorney General. Its Yes/No boxes were read by eye from the page images (the table of readings is on disk, one row per form with file and page). Each report is matched to the e-filed federal return with the same employer number and the same period end. Four answers are tested: transactions with officers or directors against Schedule L and Part IV lines 25 to 28; the audit answer against Part XII line 2b; government funding against Part VIII line 1e and, when the reporting year is a July-to-June year, against the City's payments for that fiscal year; and restricted funds against the balance sheet. City payments shown are those of the City fiscal years that overlap the reporting year.
limits: The registry files saved hold these reports for only some years (renewal packages were not downloaded), and returns e-filed before 2020 are not on disk, so most reports cannot be tested. A wrong box is usually a slip by a preparer who filled the State form from memory; the transaction itself is disclosed on the federal return, which is public. Schedule L also takes in small and ordinary dealings, such as a board member's salary as artistic director or services bought from member agencies that sit on the board. For calendar-year reports the City's fiscal-year totals cannot show in which calendar year money arrived; those rows say so. The registry can and does ask for corrections (see the next screen).
